`include()` tells Django to pull in another URL configuration instead of listing every pattern directly.  
When you write  

```python
path('blog/', include('blog.urls', namespace='blog')),
```  

the `include` call points to the `blog.urls` module, whose own `urlpatterns` list is then **inserted** under the prefix `blog/`. All of the blog app’s routes become reachable as `/blog/...` without having to copy them into the project‑level `urls.py` [1].  

Because you also pass `namespace='blog'`, the imported patterns are grouped under a unique name. That lets you refer to any blog URL elsewhere with the syntax `blog:<url_name>` (e.g., `blog:post_list`), ensuring the names don’t clash with other apps [1].  

The same pattern appears in other parts of the textbook, such as including cart, orders, and payment URLs inside `i18n_patterns` [4]. In every case, `include()` modularises the URLconf: it delegates matching to the referenced module and optionally assigns a namespace for reverse look‑ups.
